newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Christopher Plummer returns to stage to play Barrymore.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Christopher Plummer returns to stage to play Barrymore.

text.p: Christopher Plummer, one of Canada's most famous acting exports, has returned to the theater where he honed his craft -- this time to star in a play about an actor to whom he has sometimes been compared, John Barrymore.

Plummer began his association with the Stratford Festival in 1956 when he appeared in the title role of "Henry V." He has since played six seasons in leading roles at Stratford including "Hamlet," "Macbeth," "Cyrano de Bergerac," "Much Ado About Nothing" and "Antony and Cleopatra."
Plummer, 67, was born in Toronto but raised and educated in Montreal. His measured classical acting style has been compared to Sir Laurence Olivier and Barrymore.
Playing Barrymore is a particular honor, Plummer told Reuters in a telephone interview. "It is touching. It is the best play I ever read about him. It does him justice."

"Barrymore" is a William Luce play based on the life of the flamboyant actor, who started his career in 1903 and died in 1942 after playing in 60 movies and 30 plays. His private life was less illustrious. Married four times, he spent his money recklessly, drank excessively and eventually destroyed himself. Despite all that Barrymore is still considered the last of the heroic male stars of Broadway.

"He was a great hero to all of us. His glamorous life in Hollywood appealed to us as young guys," said Plummer, who has won rave reviews. "This play shows all the characteristics of Barrymore. He was funny, generous, sensitive, well-read and educated but his life was also a pain."

Plummer's professional career started in Montreal in 1944 and has spanned more than five decades. He has performed everything from Shakespeare, George Bernard Shaw and Bertold Brecht to Peter Shaffer, Neil Simon and Edmond Rostand. A television Emmy Award winner, he has also starred in films ranging from "The Return of the Pink Panther" and "The Sound of Music" to "Jesus of Nazareth" and "12 Monkeys."
"He is the best in the world," author and playwright William Luce said of Plummer. "He is a great classical actor who can get inside of Barrymore. He even looks like him."
Others associated with the Stratford festival also lavished praise on Plummer. "He is remarkable, talented, magnetic, very special and funny," said the festival's artistic director Richard Monette.

"In a sense, it is a dream and an ambition to see him here," he told Reuters in a phone interview from Stratford. "I regard him as of one the greatest stage actors of the 20th century. He is a flowering of our festival."

Plummer receives such accolades modestly. "It is a sort of second nature for me to play 'Jack' (Barrymore)," he said, adding that he returned to the stage at Stratford with good memories and a sense of bringing back to life the first half of this century.
"It is a good thing to revive this great era," he said.

In William Luce's two-hour play Barrymore is near the end of his life and on the stage at New York's Plymouth Theatre. His talent ravaged by time and drink, the once-great classical actor struggles with his failing memory in an effort to recreate a legendary performance of Richard III.

After the Stratford Festival performances which began this week and end in October, a road tour of "Barrymore" will follow to Minneapolis, Pittsburgh, Fort Lauderdale, Palm Beach, Chicago, Baltimore and Boston. The play is set to open on Broadway in March 1997.
